decks.title: Vector Algebra — Part 1: Vectors, components and the section formula
goals: Tell vectors from scalars and name the types of vectors
Find the magnitude, unit vector and direction cosines of a vector
Add vectors by the triangle and parallelogram laws and multiply by scalars
Use position vectors and the section formula

slides.heading: Vector Algebra, Part 1
slides.body_md: Quantities that need a size **and** a direction.

visual.alt: A directed line segment from the initial point A at the lower left to the terminal point B at the upper right, labelled a, with an arrowhead showing the direction from A to B.
visual.caption: The vector $\vec{a} = \overrightarrow{AB}$: its length is the magnitude $|\vec{a}|$, the arrow gives the direction.

slides.narration: Welcome to vector algebra. If a friend says the shop is two kilometres away, you still cannot find it. You also need to know which way to walk. Quantities like this, with a size and a direction, are called vectors. On the screen, an arrow from A to B is the simplest picture of a vector. In this part we learn to describe vectors with numbers and to add them.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Tell **vectors** from **scalars**; name the types of vectors
Add vectors (**triangle** and **parallelogram** laws) and multiply by scalars
slides.narration: Here are the goals for part one. We start with the difference between vectors and scalars, and the types of vectors. Then we write vectors with components and find their lengths and directions. After that we add vectors and stretch them. Finally, we locate points that divide a line segment in a given ratio, a favourite board question.

slides.heading: Scalars and vectors
slides.body_md: A **scalar** is fully described by a number with a unit. A **vector** needs a magnitude **and** a direction.

visual.alt: Table comparing scalars and vectors: mass, temperature, time and speed are scalars; displacement, velocity, force and acceleration, each with a direction, are vectors.
visual.caption: Ask: does the quantity need a direction to make sense?

slides.narration: Mass, temperature and time are scalars: one number with a unit tells you everything. Displacement, velocity, force and acceleration are vectors: you must also say which way. A speed of forty kilometres per hour is a scalar, but forty kilometres per hour towards Pune is a velocity, a vector.

slides.heading: Drawing a vector
slides.body_md: A vector is drawn as a **directed line segment** $\overrightarrow{AB}$: $A$ is the **initial point**, $B$ the **terminal point**. Its length is the **magnitude** $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$.

visual.alt: A directed line segment from the initial point A at the lower left to the terminal point B at the upper right, labelled a, with an arrowhead showing the direction from A to B.
visual.caption: The vector $\vec{a} = \overrightarrow{AB}$: its length is the magnitude $|\vec{a}|$, the arrow gives the direction.

slides.narration: We draw a vector as an arrow. It starts at the initial point A and ends at the terminal point B. The length of the arrow is the magnitude of the vector, and the arrowhead shows its direction. We name it with an arrow over the letters A B, or with a single letter such as a with a small arrow above it.

slides.heading: Types of vectors
slides.body_md: These names appear in one-mark questions. Learn the exact meaning of each.

visual.alt: Table of types of vectors: zero vector has magnitude zero; unit vector has magnitude one; coinitial vectors share an initial point; collinear vectors are parallel to one line; equal vectors have the same magnitude and direction; the negative of a vector has the same magnitude and opposite direction.
visual.caption: Six words you must use precisely.

slides.narration: The zero vector has length zero and no fixed direction. A unit vector has length one. Coinitial vectors start at the same point. Collinear vectors are parallel to the same line, whatever their lengths or senses. Equal vectors have the same length and the same direction, wherever they are drawn. The negative of a vector has the same length but points the other way.

slides.heading: Components and magnitude
slides.body_md: In space, with unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ along the axes, every vector is $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$, and $|\vec{r}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$.

visual.alt: Table of three vectors with their components and magnitudes: 2 i minus 3 j plus 6 k has magnitude 7; i plus j plus k has magnitude root 3; 4 i minus 4 j plus 2 k has magnitude 6.
visual.caption: $|x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$.

slides.narration: Three unit vectors, i hat, j hat and k hat, point along the x, y and z axes. Any vector is a combination of them, and the multipliers are its components. The magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of the components. Dividing a vector by its magnitude gives the unit vector in its direction, written with a hat.

slides.heading: Direction cosines
slides.body_md: If $\vec{r}$ makes angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with the axes, its **direction cosines** are $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$. For $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$: $l = \dfrac{x}{|\vec{r}|}$, $m = \dfrac{y}{|\vec{r}|}$, $n = \dfrac{z}{|\vec{r}|}$, and $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.

visual.alt: A sketch of three axes x, y and z from the origin O drawn in perspective, with a vector r from O to P. The angles that r makes with the x, y and z axes are marked alpha, beta and gamma. Not to scale.
visual.caption: Direction angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$; direction cosines $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: A vector makes three angles with the three axes, called alpha, beta and gamma. Their cosines are the direction cosines. You get them by dividing each component by the magnitude, so they are simply the components of the unit vector. That is why their squares always add up to one. The components themselves, or any multiple of them, are called direction ratios.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: direction cosines
slides.body_md: Find the direction cosines of $6\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1: the magnitude of 6 i minus 2 j plus 3 k is 7, the direction cosines are 6 over 7, minus 2 over 7 and 3 over 7, and their squares add up to 1.
visual.caption: Divide each component by the magnitude.

slides.narration: First find the magnitude: thirty six plus four plus nine is forty nine, and its square root is seven. Then divide each component by seven: six sevenths, minus two sevenths and three sevenths. Keep the minus sign. As a check, the squares add up to forty nine over forty nine, which is one. Without this check, small slips go unnoticed.

slides.heading: Quick check: magnitude
slides.body_md: Find the length of a vector from its components.
slides.narration: Square each component, add the squares, and take the square root. Watch out for the negative component: its square is positive.

slides.heading: Collinear vectors
slides.body_md: $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are **collinear** if $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$ for some scalar $\lambda$: their components are in the same ratio.

visual.alt: Three parallel arrows: a short arrow a, an arrow twice as long in the same direction labelled 2 a, and an arrow of the same length as a pointing the opposite way labelled minus a.
visual.caption: Collinear vectors: $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$; $\lambda > 0$ same direction, $\lambda < 0$ opposite.

slides.narration: Multiplying a vector by a number changes its length, and a negative number also reverses its direction. The result is always parallel to the original. So two vectors are collinear exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other. In components, the ratios of matching components must all be equal. A positive ratio means the same direction, a negative ratio means opposite directions.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: are they collinear?
slides.body_md: Are $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = -2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$ collinear?
bullets: **Step 3 —** The ratio is negative: they point in **opposite** directions.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 2: the ratios of the components of a to those of b are all minus three halves.
visual.caption: Equal ratios: collinear. Negative ratio: opposite directions.

slides.narration: Divide matching components. Three over minus two, minus six over four, and nine over minus six all equal minus three halves. Since every ratio is the same, a is minus three halves times b, so the vectors are collinear. The negative sign tells us more: they point in opposite directions, like the two arrows a and minus a in the earlier picture.

slides.heading: Quick check: collinear or not?
slides.body_md: Compare the components of two vectors.
slides.narration: Check whether one vector is a multiple of the other. Then look at the sign of the multiple to decide the direction.

slides.heading: Adding vectors: triangle law
slides.body_md: Place $\vec{b}$ so that it starts where $\vec{a}$ ends. Then $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ runs from the start of $\vec{a}$ to the end of $\vec{b}$. In components, add matching components.

visual.alt: Triangle law: an arrow a from O to A, then an arrow b starting where a ends, from A to B. The arrow from O straight to B, the third side of the triangle, is the sum a plus b.
visual.caption: Triangle law: $\overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{OB}$.

slides.narration: To add two vectors, place them head to tail. Walk along a from O to A, then along b from A to B. The single arrow from O to B is the sum. This is the triangle law. With components it is even simpler: add the i parts, the j parts and the k parts separately.

slides.heading: Parallelogram law
slides.body_md: If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ start at the same point, complete the parallelogram: the diagonal from that point is $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$. Also $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \vec{b} + \vec{a}$.

visual.alt: Parallelogram law: arrows a from O to A and b from O to B start at the same point. Completing the parallelogram OACB with dashed sides parallel to a and b, the diagonal from O to C is the sum a plus b.
visual.caption: Parallelogram law: the diagonal $\overrightarrow{OC} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$.

slides.narration: When the two vectors start at the same point, complete the parallelogram on them. The diagonal from the common point is their sum. The two dashed sides show why this agrees with the triangle law: the side from B to C equals a, so going along b and then a gives the same diagonal. This also shows that the order of addition does not matter.

slides.heading: Position vectors
slides.body_md: The **position vector** of $P(x, y, z)$ is $\overrightarrow{OP} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$. For points $A$, $B$ with position vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$.

visual.alt: Position vectors: from the origin O, an arrow a to the point A and an arrow b to the point B. The arrow from A to B is b minus a.
visual.caption: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$: "head minus tail".

slides.narration: Fix an origin O. The arrow from O to a point is that point’s position vector, and its components are just the coordinates of the point. To get the vector from A to B, go from A back to O and then out to B. That gives b minus a: the position vector of the head minus that of the tail.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: vector joining two points
slides.body_md: For $A(1, -2, 3)$ and $B(4, 2, 3)$, find $\overrightarrow{AB}$, its length and the unit vector along it.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 3: vector A B is 3 i plus 4 j, its length is 5, and the unit vector is three fifths i plus four fifths j.
visual.caption: Head minus tail, then divide by the length.

slides.narration: Subtract the coordinates of A from those of B: three, four and zero. So the vector from A to B is three i plus four j. Its length is the square root of nine plus sixteen, which is five. Dividing by five gives the unit vector three fifths i plus four fifths j. Notice the k component is zero: the segment is level in that direction.

slides.heading: Quick check: unit vectors
slides.body_md: Decide whether a vector has length one.
slides.narration: A unit vector has magnitude exactly one. Square the components, add them, and see whether the total is one.

slides.heading: The section formula
slides.body_md: If $R$ divides $PQ$ **internally** in the ratio $m : n$, then $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{q} + n\vec{p}}{m + n}$. **Externally:** $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{q} - n\vec{p}}{m - n}$.

visual.alt: Section formula: a segment from P to Q with the point R on it, splitting it into parts marked m and n. Dashed lines from the origin O to P, R and Q show the position vectors p, r and q.
visual.caption: $R$ divides $PQ$ in $m : n$ (drawn for $2 : 1$): $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{q} + n\vec{p}}{m + n}$.

slides.narration: Suppose R lies on the segment from P to Q and splits it in the ratio m to n. Then the position vector of R is m times q plus n times p, all over m plus n. Notice the cross pairing: m, the part next to P, multiplies q, the far end. For a point outside the segment, called external division, the plus signs become minus signs.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: internal and external division
slides.body_md: $P(1, 3, -2)$ and $Q(4, -3, 7)$. Find the points dividing $PQ$ in the ratio $1 : 2$ (a) internally (b) externally.
bullets: **Check (a) —** it is one third of the way from $P$ to $Q$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 4: dividing P Q internally in the ratio 1 to 2 gives the point (2, 1, 1); externally gives (minus 2, 9, minus 11).
visual.caption: Same ratio, two very different points.

slides.narration: Here m is one and n is two. Internally, add one times q and two times p and divide by three: the point two, one, one. Externally, subtract and divide by one minus two, which is minus one. That gives two p minus q: minus two, nine, minus eleven. This point lies on the line through P and Q, but outside the segment, on the side of P.

slides.heading: Quick check: midpoint
slides.body_md: Find the position vector of a midpoint.
slides.narration: The midpoint divides the segment in the ratio one to one. Add the two position vectors and halve the result.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Vector: magnitude and direction; scalar: magnitude only
Direction cosines $= $ components of $\hat{a}$; $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$

visual.alt: Summary flow for part one: a vector has magnitude and direction; write it in components; from components get magnitude, unit vector and direction cosines; add and scale vectors; use position vectors and the section formula.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one picture.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. A vector has a magnitude and a direction. In components, the magnitude is a square root of a sum of squares, and dividing by it gives the unit vector, whose components are the direction cosines. Collinear vectors are multiples of each other. The vector from A to B is b minus a, and the section formula locates points that divide a segment.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Always find the magnitude **before** dividing for unit vectors or direction cosines
Direction ratios are not direction cosines unless their squares add to $1$
For collinear **points**, show two vectors with a **common point** are parallel
Section formula: $m$ goes with $\vec{q}$; write "internally" or "externally"
Give vectors in the form $x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ and points as $(x, y, z)$

rows: two vectors with a common point; ratio
formula with $m$, $n$ named; internal or external

visual.alt: Exam tips table for part one: magnitude, unit vector and direction cosines carry 1 to 2 marks, show the magnitude first; collinearity carries 2 marks, show two vectors with a common point; section formula carries 2 to 3 marks, name m and n and say internal or external.
visual.caption: Where the marks are in part 1.

slides.narration: Some exam advice. Always find the magnitude first. Do not confuse direction ratios with direction cosines. To prove three points collinear, show that two vectors through a common point are parallel. In the section formula, pair m with the far end, and say whether the division is internal or external. Finally, write vectors with i, j and k, and points with brackets.

decks.title: Vector Algebra — Part 2: Dot product, cross product and their uses
goals: Find the dot product and use it for angles and perpendicularity
Find the projection of one vector on another
Find the cross product and unit vectors perpendicular to two vectors
Find areas of triangles and parallelograms with the cross product

slides.heading: Vector Algebra, Part 2
slides.body_md: Two ways to multiply vectors: one gives a number, the other a vector.

visual.alt: Projection: vector a from O to A makes an angle theta with vector b along the base line from O to B. A dashed perpendicular from A meets the base line at M with a right angle. The length OM is the projection of a on b.
visual.caption: $OM = |\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Vectors can be multiplied in two different ways. The dot product turns two vectors into a number and measures how much they point the same way. The cross product turns them into a new vector at right angles to both. On the screen, the dot product helps us find the shadow of one vector on another, called its projection.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **dot product** and the **angle** between vectors
Find the **projection** of one vector on another
Find the **cross product**, perpendicular **unit vectors** and **areas**
slides.narration: Here are the goals for part two. First the dot product, and how it gives the angle between two vectors and a quick test for right angles. Then projections. Then the cross product, which gives a vector perpendicular to two given vectors, and the areas of parallelograms and triangles.

slides.heading: The dot (scalar) product
slides.body_md: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ ($0 \le \theta \le \pi$) is the angle between them. It is a **number**. $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$.

visual.alt: Dot products of the unit vectors i, j and k: each with itself gives 1; any two different ones give 0 because they are perpendicular.
visual.caption: Same unit vector: $1$. Different unit vectors: $0$.

slides.narration: The dot product of a and b is the length of a times the length of b times the cosine of the angle between them. The answer is a number, not a vector, so it is also called the scalar product. Since i, j and k are unit vectors at right angles, each dotted with itself gives one and any two different ones give zero.

slides.heading: Dot product from components
slides.body_md: If $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = b_1\hat{i} + b_2\hat{j} + b_3\hat{k}$, then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3$. Also $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2$.

visual.alt: Table multiplying matching components of a equal to 3, minus 1, 2 and b equal to 2, 4, 1: the products are 6, minus 4 and 2, which add up to 4.
visual.caption: Multiply matching components, then add.

slides.narration: Using the table of unit vectors, the dot product in components is very simple: multiply matching components and add. For three i minus j plus two k and two i plus four j plus k, that is six minus four plus two, which is four. Rearranging the definition gives the cosine of the angle: the dot product divided by the product of the lengths.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: angle between two vectors
slides.body_md: Find the angle between $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 5: the dot product is minus 4, both magnitudes are 3, so cosine theta is minus four ninths and the angle is obtuse.
visual.caption: A negative dot product means an obtuse angle.

slides.narration: The dot product is two minus two minus four, which is minus four. Both vectors have length three. So the cosine of the angle is minus four ninths. A negative cosine means the angle is obtuse, more than a right angle. Leave the answer as the inverse cosine of minus four ninths unless the angle is a standard one.

slides.heading: Quick check: a dot product
slides.body_md: Multiply matching components and add.
slides.narration: Line up the i, j and k parts, multiply each pair, and add the three products. Take care with the negative component.

slides.heading: Perpendicular vectors
slides.body_md: For non-zero vectors, $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$ exactly when $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$ (since $\cos 90° = 0$).

visual.alt: Two arrows a and b leaving the same point O at a right angle, marked with a small square at O.
visual.caption: $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b} \iff \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$ (for non-zero vectors).

slides.narration: If the angle is a right angle, its cosine is zero, so the dot product is zero. The reverse is also true for non-zero vectors. This gives the fastest test for perpendicular vectors, and a way to find an unknown component: set the dot product equal to zero and solve.

slides.heading: Projection of a vector on another
slides.body_md: The **projection** of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ is $|\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = \vec{a} \cdot \hat{b}$. It is negative when $\theta$ is obtuse.

visual.alt: Projection: vector a from O to A makes an angle theta with vector b along the base line from O to B. A dashed perpendicular from A meets the base line at M with a right angle. The length OM is the projection of a on b.
visual.caption: $OM = |\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$.

slides.narration: Drop a perpendicular from the end of a onto the line of b. The length from O to the foot M is the projection of a on b. It equals the length of a times cosine theta, which is the dot product divided by the length of b. Divide by the length of the vector you are projecting on, not the other one.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: projection
slides.body_md: Find the projection of $\vec{a} = 4\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ on $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 6: the dot product is 9, the length of b is 3, so the projection of a on b is 3.
visual.caption: Divide by the length of the vector you project **on**.

slides.narration: The dot product is eight minus two plus three, which is nine. We project on b, so we divide by the length of b, which is three. The projection is three. If you divided by the length of a instead, you would get the projection of b on a, a different number.

slides.heading: Quick check: angle
slides.body_md: Find the angle between two simple vectors.
slides.narration: Find the dot product, then the two lengths, then the cosine. Match the cosine with a standard angle.

slides.heading: Useful expansions
slides.body_md: The dot product distributes over addition, so magnitudes of sums can be expanded like squares.

visual.alt: Table of expansions: the square of the length of a plus b is length a squared plus twice a dot b plus length b squared; for a minus b the middle sign is minus; a plus b dotted with a minus b is length a squared minus length b squared.
visual.caption: They work because $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$.

slides.narration: Because the dot product of a vector with itself is the square of its length, you can expand the length of a plus b squared just like an algebraic square. The middle term is twice a dot b. With a minus b, the middle sign changes. And a plus b dotted with a minus b is the difference of the squares of the lengths.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: angle from magnitudes
slides.body_md: $|\vec{a}| = 2$, $|\vec{b}| = 5$ and $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = \sqrt{19}$. Find the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

visual.alt: Flow for worked example 7: from the given lengths, expand the square of the length of a plus b to get a dot b equal to minus 5, then cosine theta is minus one half and theta is 120 degrees.
visual.caption: Square the magnitude, expand, solve for the dot product.

slides.narration: We do not know the components, only lengths. Square the length of a plus b and expand: nineteen equals four plus twice a dot b plus twenty five. So a dot b is minus five. The cosine of the angle is minus five over ten, which is minus one half, and the angle is two pi over three, or one hundred and twenty degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: perpendicular?
slides.body_md: Use the dot product test.
slides.narration: Compute the dot product. If it is zero, and neither vector is zero, the vectors are perpendicular.

slides.heading: The cross (vector) product
slides.body_md: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to both, given by the **right-hand rule**. It is a **vector**, and $\vec{b} \times \vec{a} = -\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$.

visual.alt: Cross products of the unit vectors, row times column: i cross j is k, j cross k is i, k cross i is j; the reverse orders give the negatives; any unit vector crossed with itself is the zero vector.
visual.caption: Cyclic order $\hat{i} \to \hat{j} \to \hat{k} \to \hat{i}$ gives $+$; against it gives $-$.

slides.narration: The cross product of a and b is a vector. Its length is the length of a times the length of b times sine theta, and it points at right angles to both a and b. Curl the fingers of your right hand from a towards b: your thumb shows the direction. Swapping the order reverses it. For unit vectors, go round the cycle i, j, k for a plus sign.

slides.heading: Cross product from components
slides.body_md: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)\hat{i} + (a_3b_1 - a_1b_3)\hat{j} + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)\hat{k}$. Parallel vectors give $\vec{0}$.

visual.alt: Table of the component formula for a cross b, worked for a equal to 1, 2, minus 1 and b equal to 2, minus 1, 3: the components are 5, minus 5 and minus 5.
visual.caption: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = 5\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$.

slides.narration: In components, each part of the cross product is a difference of two cross products of the other components. A good way to remember it is the pattern you will see with determinants, expanded along the row i, j, k. Always check your answer: the dot product of the result with a, and with b, must be zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: unit vector perpendicular to two vectors
slides.body_md: Find the unit vectors perpendicular to both $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 8: a cross b is 5 i minus 5 j minus 5 k, its magnitude is 5 root 3, so the unit vectors perpendicular to both are plus or minus one over root 3 times i minus j minus k.
visual.caption: Two answers: the normal can point either way.

slides.narration: The cross product is five i minus five j minus five k. Its length is the square root of seventy five, which is five root three. Dividing gives one over root three times i minus j minus k. There are two answers, with a plus or minus sign, because a perpendicular can point either way. The check shows the result is perpendicular to both vectors.

slides.heading: Area with the cross product
slides.body_md: The parallelogram with adjacent sides $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ has area $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$. The triangle with sides $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ has area $\dfrac12|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$.

visual.alt: A parallelogram OACB with sides a along the base and b slanting up at angle theta. A dashed height from B drops to H on the base with a right angle; the height equals the length of b times sine theta.
visual.caption: Area $= |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\sin\theta = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$; the triangle $OAB$ has half of it.

slides.narration: Here is why the cross product measures area. A parallelogram has area base times height. The base is the length of a, and the height is the length of b times sine theta. Their product is exactly the length of a cross b. A triangle on the same two sides is half of the parallelogram, so its area is half the length of a cross b.

notes.title: Vector Algebra — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Vectors, scalars and types of vectors
sections.body_md:
A **scalar** has magnitude only (mass, time, temperature, speed). A **vector** has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force). A vector is drawn as a directed line segment $\overrightarrow{AB}$ from the **initial point** $A$ to the **terminal point** $B$; its length $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$ is its **magnitude**.

**Types:** zero vector ($|\vec{0}| = 0$, direction arbitrary); unit vector (magnitude $1$); coinitial vectors (same initial point); collinear vectors (parallel to one line, whatever their magnitudes or senses); equal vectors (same magnitude **and** direction); negative of a vector (same magnitude, opposite direction): $\overrightarrow{BA} = -\overrightarrow{AB}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A quantity with magnitude and direction.
Vectors with the same magnitude and the same direction, wherever they are drawn.
Vectors parallel to the same line.

visual.alt: Table of types of vectors: zero vector has magnitude zero; unit vector has magnitude one; coinitial vectors share an initial point; collinear vectors are parallel to one line; equal vectors have the same magnitude and direction; the negative of a vector has the same magnitude and opposite direction.
visual.caption: Six words you must use precisely.

sections.heading: 2. Components, magnitude and direction cosines
sections.body_md:
With unit vectors $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ along the axes, $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ has **components** $x, y, z$ and magnitude $|\vec{r}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$. The **unit vector** along $\vec{a}$ is $\hat{a} = \dfrac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$.

If $\vec{r}$ makes angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with the positive axes, its **direction cosines** are $l = \cos\alpha = \dfrac{x}{|\vec{r}|}$, $m = \cos\beta = \dfrac{y}{|\vec{r}|}$, $n = \cos\gamma = \dfrac{z}{|\vec{r}|}$, and $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$. Numbers proportional to $l, m, n$ (such as $x, y, z$) are **direction ratios**.

Example: $6\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ has magnitude $7$ and direction cosines $\dfrac67, -\dfrac27, \dfrac37$.

key_terms.definition_md: Cosines of the angles a vector makes with the three axes.
Any three numbers proportional to the direction cosines.

visual.alt: A sketch of three axes x, y and z from the origin O drawn in perspective, with a vector r from O to P. The angles that r makes with the x, y and z axes are marked alpha, beta and gamma. Not to scale.
visual.caption: Direction angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$; direction cosines $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$ (sketch, not to scale).

sections.heading: 3. Addition and scalar multiplication
sections.body_md:
**Triangle law:** $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$. **Parallelogram law:** for coinitial $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, the diagonal of the parallelogram on them is $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$. Addition is commutative and associative; $\vec{a} + \vec{0} = \vec{a}$; $\vec{a} + (-\vec{a}) = \vec{0}$. Around a closed triangle $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} + \overrightarrow{CA} = \vec{0}$.

**Scalar multiple:** $\lambda\vec{a}$ has magnitude $|\lambda||\vec{a}|$, the same direction as $\vec{a}$ if $\lambda > 0$ and the opposite if $\lambda < 0$. In components, add (or multiply) component by component.

**Collinear test:** $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are collinear iff $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$, i.e. $\dfrac{b_1}{a_1} = \dfrac{b_2}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_3}{a_3}$ (zero components must match).

key_terms.definition_md: Head-to-tail addition: the third side is the sum.
$\lambda\vec{a}$: length scaled by $|\lambda|$, direction reversed if $\lambda < 0$.

visual.alt: Parallelogram law: arrows a from O to A and b from O to B start at the same point. Completing the parallelogram OACB with dashed sides parallel to a and b, the diagonal from O to C is the sum a plus b.
visual.caption: Parallelogram law: the diagonal $\overrightarrow{OC} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$.

visuals.alt: Three parallel arrows: a short arrow a, an arrow twice as long in the same direction labelled 2 a, and an arrow of the same length as a pointing the opposite way labelled minus a.
visuals.caption: Collinear vectors: $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$; $\lambda > 0$ same direction, $\lambda < 0$ opposite.

sections.heading: 4. Position vectors and the section formula
sections.body_md:
The position vector of $P(x, y, z)$ is $\overrightarrow{OP} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$. For any two points, $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$ ("head minus tail").

If $R$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $m : n$:
- **internally:** $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{q} + n\vec{p}}{m + n}$;
- **externally:** $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{q} - n\vec{p}}{m - n}$;
- **midpoint:** $\vec{r} = \dfrac{\vec{p} + \vec{q}}{2}$.

**Collinear points** $A, B, C$: show $\overrightarrow{AB} = \lambda\overrightarrow{AC}$ (parallel vectors with the common point $A$).

Example: $P(1, 3, -2)$, $Q(4, -3, 7)$, ratio $1 : 2$: internal point $(2, 1, 1)$, external point $(-2, 9, -11)$.

key_terms.definition_md: The vector from the origin to the point.
The dividing point lies on line PQ but outside the segment.

visual.alt: Section formula: a segment from P to Q with the point R on it, splitting it into parts marked m and n. Dashed lines from the origin O to P, R and Q show the position vectors p, r and q.
visual.caption: $R$ divides $PQ$ in $m : n$ (drawn for $2 : 1$): $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{q} + n\vec{p}}{m + n}$.

visuals.alt: Position vectors: from the origin O, an arrow a to the point A and an arrow b to the point B. The arrow from A to B is b minus a.
visuals.caption: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$: "head minus tail".

sections.heading: 5. Dot product, angle and projection
sections.body_md:
$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3$, a scalar, with $0 \le \theta \le \pi$.

**Properties:** $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$; $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}$; $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2$; $\hat{i} \cdot \hat{i} = 1$, $\hat{i} \cdot \hat{j} = 0$.

**Angle:** $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|}$. **Perpendicular** (non-zero vectors): $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$. Positive dot product: acute angle; negative: obtuse.

**Projection** of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$: $\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$; the vector component of $\vec{a}$ along $\vec{b}$ is this number times $\hat{b}$.

**Expansions:** $|\vec{a} \pm \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 \pm 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + |\vec{b}|^2$; $(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a} - \vec{b}) = |\vec{a}|^2 - |\vec{b}|^2$.

key_terms.definition_md: The signed length of the shadow of one vector on the line of another.

visual.alt: Projection: vector a from O to A makes an angle theta with vector b along the base line from O to B. A dashed perpendicular from A meets the base line at M with a right angle. The length OM is the projection of a on b.
visual.caption: $OM = |\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$.

visuals.alt: Table of expansions: the square of the length of a plus b is length a squared plus twice a dot b plus length b squared; for a minus b the middle sign is minus; a plus b dotted with a minus b is length a squared minus length b squared.
visuals.caption: They work because $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$.

sections.heading: 6. Cross product, perpendicular vectors and areas
sections.body_md:
$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ (right-hand rule).

**Components:** $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)\hat{i} + (a_3b_1 - a_1b_3)\hat{j} + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)\hat{k}$.

**Properties:** $\vec{b} \times \vec{a} = -\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$; $\vec{a} \times \vec{a} = \vec{0}$; non-zero $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0}$ iff $\vec{a} \parallel \vec{b}$; $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$; $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 + (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^2 = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$.

**Unit vectors perpendicular to both:** $\pm\dfrac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}$.

**Areas:** parallelogram with adjacent sides $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$: $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$; with diagonals $\vec{d_1}, \vec{d_2}$: $\dfrac12|\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2}|$; triangle $ABC$: $\dfrac12|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}|$.

key_terms.definition_md: A vector of length $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin\theta$ perpendicular to both.
Fingers curl from $\vec{a}$ to $\vec{b}$; the thumb gives the direction of $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$.

visual.alt: A parallelogram OACB with sides a along the base and b slanting up at angle theta. A dashed height from B drops to H on the base with a right angle; the height equals the length of b times sine theta.
visual.caption: Area $= |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\sin\theta = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$; the triangle $OAB$ has half of it.

visuals.alt: Cross products of the unit vectors, row times column: i cross j is k, j cross k is i, k cross i is j; the reverse orders give the negatives; any unit vector crossed with itself is the zero vector.
visuals.caption: Cyclic order $\hat{i} \to \hat{j} \to \hat{k} \to \hat{i}$ gives $+$; against it gives $-$.

sections.heading: 7. Choosing the right tool
sections.body_md:
- Length or direction of one vector: magnitude, unit vector, direction cosines.
- Points on a line, ratios: position vectors, section formula, collinearity.
- Angles, right angles, shadows, work done ($W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$): **dot product**.
- A direction at right angles to two vectors, areas: **cross product**.

Check your work: a unit vector has magnitude $1$; direction cosines square-sum to $1$; a cross product dots to $0$ with both factors; an area is positive.

key_terms.definition_md: $\vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$ for a constant force through a displacement.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Objective (1 mark):* magnitude, unit vector, direction cosines, a dot or cross product, a value of $\lambda$.
- *Short answer (2–3 marks):* method step (formula written) + correct working + final answer in vector form.
- *Long answer (5 marks):* several connected parts (angle, projection, cross product, area); each part carries its own step mark.
- *Case-based (4 marks):* read the vectors from the situation, then apply the right product.

**Common mistakes**
1. Dividing by the wrong magnitude in a projection.
2. Giving direction ratios when direction cosines are asked.
3. Pairing $m$ with $\vec{p}$ instead of $\vec{q}$ in the section formula.
4. Using $\vec{a} - \vec{b}$ for $\overrightarrow{AB}$ (it is $\vec{b} - \vec{a}$).
5. Sign errors in the $\hat{j}$ component of a cross product.
6. Forgetting the $\pm$ for perpendicular unit vectors.
7. Forgetting to halve for the area of a triangle (or halving for a parallelogram).
8. Treating $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ and $\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$ as equal.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.solution_md: Displacement has both a size and a direction (for example 3 km towards the north-east). Mass, temperature and time are fully described by a number with a unit, so they are scalars.

questions.stem_md: The magnitude of $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$ is
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-3)^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. The value $49$ forgets the square root; $5$ adds the components; $\sqrt{19}$ forgets to square the $6$.

questions.stem_md: The unit vector in the direction of $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{k}$ is
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, so $\hat{a} = \dfrac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|} = \dfrac{3}{5}\hat{i} + \dfrac{4}{5}\hat{k}$. Dividing by $3 + 4 = 7$ is a common slip; the $\hat{j}$ version changes the direction.

questions.stem_md: The direction cosines of the vector $\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ are
questions.solution_md: Magnitude $\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$. Direction cosines are the components divided by $3$: $\dfrac13, -\dfrac23, \dfrac23$. The numbers $1, -2, 2$ are direction ratios; the last option points the opposite way.

questions.stem_md: A non-zero vector makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the positive $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes. Then $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma$ equals
questions.solution_md: If $l, m, n$ are the direction cosines of $\vec{r}$, then $l\hat{i} + m\hat{j} + n\hat{k}$ is the unit vector $\hat{r}$, whose magnitude is $1$. So $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.

questions.stem_md: The vectors $2\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$ and $-\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ are

options.text_md: collinear and in the same direction

questions.solution_md: $2\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 6\hat{k} = -2(-\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k})$: one is a negative multiple of the other, so they are collinear and point in opposite directions. (Their dot product is $-28 \ne 0$, so they are not perpendicular.)

questions.stem_md: For which positive value of $p$ is $p(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$ a unit vector?
questions.solution_md: $|p(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})| = p\sqrt{3}$ for $p > 0$. Setting $p\sqrt{3} = 1$ gives $p = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

questions.stem_md: If $A(1, 2, -1)$ and $B(3, -2, 5)$, then $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\overrightarrow{AB}$ = position vector of $B$ minus position vector of $A$ $= (3 - 1)\hat{i} + (-2 - 2)\hat{j} + (5 + 1)\hat{k}$. Subtracting the other way round gives the negative vector; adding gives neither.

questions.stem_md: The position vector of the midpoint of the segment joining $P(2, -1, 4)$ and $Q(4, 3, -2)$ is
questions.solution_md: Midpoint $= \dfrac{\vec{p} + \vec{q}}{2} = \dfrac{6\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}}{2}$. Half of $\vec{q} - \vec{p}$ is a displacement, not a position.

questions.stem_md: Points $P$ and $Q$ have position vectors $\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $4\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$. The point $R$ dividing $PQ$ internally in the ratio $2 : 1$ has position vector
questions.solution_md: $\vec{r} = \dfrac{2\vec{q} + 1\cdot\vec{p}}{2 + 1} = \dfrac{9\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}}{3}$. Pairing the $2$ with $\vec{p}$ instead of $\vec{q}$ gives the point that divides in $1 : 2$; forgetting to divide by $3$ gives the last option.

questions.stem_md: For any triangle $ABC$, $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} + \overrightarrow{CA}$ equals
questions.solution_md: By the triangle law, $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$, and $\overrightarrow{AC} + \overrightarrow{CA} = \vec{0}$: going round the triangle brings you back to the start.

questions.stem_md: If $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is
questions.solution_md: Multiply matching components and add: $3(2) + (-1)(4) + 2(1) = 6 - 4 + 2 = 4$. Ignoring the minus sign gives $12$.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\lambda$ for which $2\hat{i} + \lambda\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ is perpendicular to $\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ is
questions.solution_md: Perpendicular means the dot product is zero: $2 - 2\lambda + 3 = 0$, so $\lambda = \dfrac52$.

questions.stem_md: The angle between $\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|} = \dfrac{0 + 1 + 0}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac12$, so $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: The projection of $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ on $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ is
questions.solution_md: Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ $= \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = \dfrac{2 + 6 - 2}{3} = 2$. Dividing by $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{14}$ gives the projection of $\vec{b}$ on $\vec{a}$ instead.

questions.stem_md: $\hat{k} \times \hat{j}$ equals
questions.solution_md: In the cyclic order $\hat{i} \to \hat{j} \to \hat{k} \to \hat{i}$, $\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}$. Reversing the order changes the sign, so $\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}$. A cross product is a vector, never the number $1$.

questions.stem_md: If $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, then $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (1 - 1)\hat{i} - (1 + 2)\hat{j} + (-1 - 2)\hat{k} = -3\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$, whose magnitude is $\sqrt{9 + 9} = 3\sqrt{2}$. ($18$ forgets the square root.)

questions.stem_md: The diagonals of a parallelogram are $3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$. Its area is
questions.solution_md: For diagonals $\vec{d_1}$, $\vec{d_2}$ the area is $\dfrac12|\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2}|$. Here $\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2} = -2\hat{i} - 14\hat{j} - 10\hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt{3}$; half of it is $5\sqrt{3}$. Forgetting the half gives $10\sqrt{3}$.

questions.stem_md: If $|\vec{a}| = 3$, $|\vec{b}| = 4$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 6$, then $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|$ is
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + |\vec{b}|^2 = 9 + 12 + 16 = 37$. Note $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = 7$ only if the vectors point the same way; $\sqrt{13}$ is $|\vec{a} - \vec{b}|$.

questions.stem_md: A vector $\vec{r}$ of magnitude $8$ makes an angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ with the $x$-axis, $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ with the $y$-axis and an acute angle $\gamma$ with the $z$-axis. Find $\gamma$ and $\vec{r}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\cos^2\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \cos^2\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \cos^2\gamma = 1$, so $\dfrac12 + \dfrac14 + \cos^2\gamma = 1$ and $\cos^2\gamma = \dfrac14$.

$\gamma$ is acute, so $\cos\gamma = \dfrac12$ and $\gamma = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

$\vec{r} = 8\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i} + \dfrac12\hat{j} + \dfrac12\hat{k}\right) = 4\sqrt{2}\,\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$.

questions.stem_md:
Let $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{k}$.

(a) Find $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ and the cosine of the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

(b) Find the projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$.

(c) Find $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ and the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

(d) Verify that $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 + (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})^2 = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 6 + 0 - 8 = -2$; $|\vec{a}| = 3$, $|\vec{b}| = 5$, so $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{2}{15}$ (an obtuse angle).

(b) Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ $= \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = -\dfrac25$.

(c) $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = (1 \cdot 4 - 0)\hat{i} - (8 + 6)\hat{j} + (0 - 3)\hat{k} = 4\hat{i} - 14\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$. Area $= \sqrt{16 + 196 + 9} = \sqrt{221}$ square units.

(d) $221 + 4 = 225$ and $|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2 = 9 \times 25 = 225$. Verified.

questions.stem_md:
The points $P$ and $Q$ have position vectors $2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $8\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$.

(a) Find the position vector of $R$, which divides $PQ$ internally in the ratio $1 : 2$.

(b) Find the position vector of $S$, which divides $PQ$ externally in the ratio $1 : 2$.

(c) Find $|\overrightarrow{SR}|$ and the direction cosines of $\overrightarrow{SR}$.

(d) Is $P$ the midpoint of $SR$? Justify your answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\vec{r} = \dfrac{1\cdot\vec{q} + 2\vec{p}}{3} = \dfrac{12\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}}{3} = 4\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

(b) $\vec{s} = \dfrac{1\cdot\vec{q} - 2\vec{p}}{1 - 2} = 2\vec{p} - \vec{q} = -4\hat{i} - 7\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}$.

(c) $\overrightarrow{SR} = \vec{r} - \vec{s} = 8\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}$, so $|\overrightarrow{SR}| = 8\sqrt{3}$; direction cosines $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

(d) Midpoint of $SR$ $= \dfrac{\vec{s} + \vec{r}}{2} = -3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$, which is not $\vec{p}$. So $P$ is **not** the midpoint (it divides $SR$ in the ratio $3 : 1$).

$A(1, 1, 2)$, $B(2, 3, 5)$ and $C(1, 5, 5)$ are the vertices of a triangle.

(a) Find the area of triangle $ABC$.

(b) Find $\cos A$.

(c) Hence, or otherwise, find the length of the perpendicular from $C$ to the line $AB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\overrightarrow{AB} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, $\overrightarrow{AC} = 4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.
$\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = (6 - 12)\hat{i} - (3 - 0)\hat{j} + (4 - 0)\hat{k} = -6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, magnitude $\sqrt{36 + 9 + 16} = \sqrt{61}$. Area $= \dfrac{\sqrt{61}}{2}$ square units.

(b) $\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = 0 + 8 + 9 = 17$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{14}$, $|\overrightarrow{AC}| = 5$. $\cos A = \dfrac{17}{5\sqrt{14}}$.

(c) Area $= \dfrac12 \times AB \times h$, so $h = \dfrac{2 \times \text{area}}{AB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{61}}{\sqrt{14}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{61}{14}}$ units (about $2.09$).

(b) $\vec{b_1}$ is the projection times $\hat{a}$: $\vec{b_1} = 2 \cdot \dfrac{\vec{a}}{3} = \dfrac23\hat{i} + \dfrac43\hat{j} + \dfrac43\hat{k}$.
$\vec{b_2} = \vec{b} - \vec{b_1} = \dfrac{10}{3}\hat{i} + \dfrac{2}{3}\hat{j} - \dfrac{7}{3}\hat{k}$.

(c) $\vec{b_2} \cdot \vec{a} = \dfrac{10}{3} + \dfrac43 - \dfrac{14}{3} = 0$ ✓. $|\vec{b_1}|^2 = 4$, $|\vec{b_2}|^2 = \dfrac{100 + 4 + 49}{9} = 17$, and $4 + 17 = 21 = |\vec{b}|^2$ ✓.

(a) Find $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$.

(b) Find the vector $\vec{d}$ that is perpendicular to both $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ and satisfies $\vec{c} \cdot \vec{d} = 20$.

(c) Find the area of the triangle that has $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ as two of its sides.

answer.model_answer_md:

(b) Any vector perpendicular to both is $\vec{d} = \lambda(2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})$. Then $\vec{c} \cdot \vec{d} = \lambda(2 + 5 + 3) = 10\lambda = 20$, so $\lambda = 2$ and $\vec{d} = 4\hat{i} + 10\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$.
Check: $\vec{d} \cdot \vec{a} = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0$ and $\vec{d} \cdot \vec{b} = 8 + 10 - 18 = 0$.

(c) Area $= \dfrac12|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = \dfrac12\sqrt{4 + 25 + 9} = \dfrac{\sqrt{38}}{2}$ square units.
